analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the corporate income tax and all taxes on capital gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set the corporate income tax rate to zero, cut the tax rate on capital gains to zero percent for both individuals and corporations, and extend for one year a tax break letting businesses immediately deduct the full cost of equipment purchases. The corporate rate cut would begin with tax years after December 31, 2011, and the capital gains cuts would apply to tax years ending after the bill's enactment [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Paul Broun with eight Republican cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action on it [S1] [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, which would stop paying federal income tax entirely, and shareholders and other investors, who would pay nothing on the profits they make from selling assets. The largest gains would go to the biggest corporations and the wealthiest households, since they own most corporate stock and realize most capital gains. Capital-intensive businesses would also gain from another year of being able to fully deduct equipment purchases upfront [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to set the corporate income tax rate at 0 percent of taxable income, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2011 [S3].

It sets the capital gains rate at 0 percent for both individuals and corporations, and repeals the scheduled sunset of the reduced capital gains rates from the 2003 tax law so the cut would not expire [S2] [S3].

It extends for one year the additional (bonus) depreciation allowance, the 100 percent expensing allowance for business and investment assets, and the option to accelerate alternative minimum tax credits in lieu of bonus depreciation [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Because the bill contains no replacement revenue, eliminating corporate and capital gains taxes would create very large federal deficits, which over time are borne by taxpayers through borrowing costs, inflation of the debt burden, or eventual spending cuts and tax increases elsewhere. Whatever growth the tax cuts produced would not be enough to offset the loss of an entire revenue stream, so ordinary taxpayers would ultimately bear the cost of the hole the bill creates.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no offsetting revenue, so eliminating the corporate income tax and capital gains taxes would produce very large federal deficits; corporate taxes are roughly a tenth of federal revenue, and the capital gains tax falls almost entirely on the top income earners who own most assets.

Because capital gains and corporate profits flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, the tax cut is concentrated there; the CRS summary identifies the beneficiaries as corporations and owners of capital, not wage earners [S2].

Even supporters of lower business taxes generally paired rate cuts with base-broadening to keep the change revenue-neutral; this bill contains no such trade, making its fiscal effect a straight transfer to asset owners paid for by future taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would flow almost entirely to corporations and wealthy asset holders, while the cost — the loss of the entire corporate income tax and capital gains tax — would fall on the federal budget and eventually on everyone else through deficits or offsetting taxes and cuts. Whatever investment stimulus the cuts produced would come at the price of the largest single-direction tax cut in modern history, with no mechanism to pay for it. The bill as written is a pure transfer to concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun introduced the bill on February 11, 2011, with eight original cosponsors, all Republicans [S1] [S3].

The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever taken [S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, corporations and wealthy asset holders did not receive the tax elimination it offered, and the federal budget avoided the very large revenue loss it would have created. Ordinary taxpayers are better off relative to the bill's passage, since they would have eventually borne the cost of the unfunded cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who avoided the unfunded cuts

for.name: Rep. Paul Broun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate corporate and capital gains taxes

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the corporate income tax and capital gains taxes entirely, but it was never enacted, so these interests gained nothing. Had it passed, the benefit would have flowed overwhelmingly to them at public expense through lost federal revenue.

These industries use bonus depreciation most heavily and would have gained a year of full upfront equipment deduction, but the bill died before the extension took effect. The public cost of the extension would have been added to the deficit.
The Treasury keeps the revenue from corporate and capital gains taxes that the bill would have eliminated. Had it passed, the shortfall would have been borne by future taxpayers.
